questions.question: Explain why conventional symbols are needed on a 1:50 000 topographic map and describe the three forms of symbol and the five main colours, giving an example of each form.
questions.expected_answer: At 1:50 000 most features are too small to draw to scale, so standard, enlarged and simplified symbols explained in the key are used and are the same on every sheet. Point symbols mark features at one place (building, windmill, trig station); line symbols show long narrow features (river, road, railway, power line); area symbols cover regions (dam, plantation, cultivated land). Blue shows water, brown relief, green vegetation, red main roads and black most constructed features and lettering.

questions.question: Distinguish between natural and constructed features, giving three examples of each, and explain why a dam is classed as constructed.
questions.expected_answer: Natural features are formed by natural processes, for example perennial or non-perennial rivers, marshes, pans, cliffs, dongas and indigenous forest. Constructed features are made by people, for example roads, railways, buildings, furrows, windmills, cultivated land and plantations. A dam is constructed because people built the wall across the river that stores the water; without it there would be only a river.

questions.question: Use symbols to identify evidence for irrigation farming and for extensive stock farming, and explain each piece of evidence.
questions.expected_answer: Irrigation: a furrow leading from the river and cultivated land on the flat floodplain beside it, perhaps a weir across the river, show water being diverted to crops. Stock farming: many windmills pumping groundwater for livestock, scattered farmsteads and few cultivated lands, often with non-perennial rivers, show a dry area where land is used for grazing rather than crops.
